newsitem.title: MEXICO: Single gunman killed Mexico's Colosio - officials.
newsitem.headline: Single gunman killed Mexico's Colosio - officials.

text.p: More than three years after Mexico's worst political assasination in decades, authorities have returned to a hypothesis that a single shooter killed presidential candidate Luis Donaldo Colosio.

However, officials still believe confessed gunman Mario Aburto Martinez may have been part of a larger conspiracy to kill Colosio, special investigator Luis Raul Gonzalez Perez told a news conference late on Thursday.
"We are investigating possible accomplices including intellectual authors of the crime," Gonzalez Perez said.
"What we can say, with evidence in hand, is that only one person pulled the trigger on a gun that took the life of the presidential candidate," he said.

Colosio was shot twice, including once in the head, at a campaign rally on March 23, 1994, in the northern border city of Tijuana. As the ruling party candidate, he was the clear front-runner for the country's top post.

Colosio's murder is to Mexico what the John F. Kennedy assasination is to the United States. The killing roiled Mexico's political system, caused widespread disillusionment with the government and spawned numerous conspiracy theories.

Much to the dismay of Mexicans, authorities have been unable to solve the case. They first said Aburto acted alone, then said it was a larger conspiracy and arrested scores of accomplices including another alleged gunman, Othon Cortes. Four different government prosecutors have handled the case.

After more than a year in jail, Cortes was freed last year by a judge who ruled there was insufficient evidence against him. Other suspects were also freed and Aburto, serving a 45-year sentence, is the only man in prison for the killing.

Following 87 new scientific tests and 305 different testimonies, new investigators believed Aburto fired both shots from the same gun at Colosio -- a fatal shot to the head and, two seconds later, another shot at his abdomen.
The case's previous investigator maintained that Aburto could not have shot Colosio twice because both bullets entered the candidate's body from different directions.

But Gonzalez Perez said that Colosio had begun to turn to his left at the moment he was shot in the head. When he was shot, he bounced off a person standing near him, and turned further as he hit the ground. It was then Aburto fired the second shot, he said.
Opposition legislators immediately cast doubt upon the finding, suggesting authorities were trying to return to a lone killer theory to cover up any official involvement.
